packages.title: Discrete event stimulation toolset to perform cost effectiveness analysis for health economics
packages.description:
WARDEN is a user-friendly package that facilitates the use of discrete event simulations with or without resource constraints for cost-effectiveness analysis. The package supports a flexible, transparent, practical approach to discrete event simulation while keeping an acceptable performance.

The current version supports:

Discrete event simulation models, Markov/semi-Markov models and hybrid models using parallel and non-parallel engines
Constrained and unconstrained models (with or without interactivity between patients)
Seamlessly integrating data.frames and other objects into the model
Delayed execution of the main inputs to facilitate readability of the model
Implementation of structural and parameter uncertainty
Helper functions to facilitate drawing of time to events and the use of hazard ratios, as well as other functions to facilitate transparency
Performing cost-effectiveness and uncertainty analysis
packages.use_cases: Perform resource constrained and unconstrained discrete event stimulation cost effectiveness models
packages.unique_features: User friendly, many helper functions, easy to implement and debug

packages.title: Fitting distributions with parameter uncertainty using the objective Bayesian method of calibrating priors
packages.description:
This package is to help climate scientists, actuaries and other risk modellers fit distributions and regression models, but including parameter uncertainty. Including parameter uncertainty gives predictive distributions that give well calibrated probabilities and return levels of future data points.
This compares with standard methods for fitting distributions, such as maxlik, which ignore parameter uncertainty, and underestimate the probabilities of future extremes. 
The methods in this package either eliminate this underestimation, or greatly reduce it (depending on the model).

The package provides the usual methods (d for density, p for probability, q for quantiles and r for random deviates).
It’s fast and straightforward to use.
It’s the only package that provides such easy-to-use functionality for fitting predictive distributions, and the only package that provides routines for testing the calibration of fitted distributions.

There are 3 related journal papers, in climate, actuarial and statistical journals:

https://doi.org/10.5194/ascmo-11-1-2025
https://doi.org/10.1017/S1748499525100237
https://doi.org/10.3390/stats8040109
packages.use_cases:
In climate science: modelling the probability distribution of annual maximum temperatures in London based on data from the last 70 years, with the goal of understanding the probabilities of what might happen next year

In actuarial science: modelling the probability distribution of losses to an insurance portfolio based on losses from the last 20 years, with the goal of understanding the probabilities of what might happen next year
packages.similar_packages:
Similar to fitdistrplus, but includes parameter uncertainty, and so produces predictive distributions, not just best fit distributions.

Similar to the various other extreme value packages in R (such as extRemes, evd, evir, climextRemes, extremeStat, fExtremes) but makes it possible (or at least easier) to include objective parameter uncertainty, which is necessary for well calibrated probabilities. 

Similar to the various Bayesian packages in R (such as extRemes, MCMC4Extremes, revdbayes, texmex) but faster because it uses asymptotic expansions, and easier because you don't have to specify a prior, or burn-in or convergence criteria.  

A slightly simplified version of fitdistcp is also available in Python.
packages.unique_features:
This is the only package that provides straightforward commands for fitting distributions with parameter uncertainty, i.e. predictive distributions.
Including parameter uncertainty is essential when distributions are being for risk assessment.

packages.title: Perform mutation testing on test suites of packages to assess the test suite's effectiveness
packages.description:
mutator is an automated mutation testing tool for the R language. It applies mutation testing principles to help developers improve test suite quality by introducing small, systematic changes (mutations) to source code, creating mutants, and verifying if tests can detect these changes. It can then compute the mutation score, i.e the number of mutants detected by the test suite over the total number of mutants.
It is fast, detect semantically equivalent mutants that would skew the scores, and honour covr annotations.
packages.use_cases:
- assess the effectiveness of a package test suite
- participate to the validation of a package
- adds a mutation testing workflow for your package CI/CD
packages.unique_features: Compared to muttest, mutator is faster, supports equivalent mutant detection, test suites that do not use testthat, and covr annotations.

packages.title: Download, cache, and analyze 40 years of CDC BRFSS survey microdata with era-correct survey weights
packages.description:
BRFSS is the largest continuously conducted health telephone survey in the world, but getting it into R has never been easy. CDC publishes each year as a SAS Transport file inside a ZIP archive, 300-plus columns wide, with variable names that drift across years, value labels that live only in PDF codebooks, and a weighting methodology break at 2011 that makes earlier and later estimates non-comparable. The usual workflow is to hand-download a ZIP, read it with haven, guess which weight column applies, and rebuild the survey design code from scratch every project.

brfssdata replaces that with three lines. Every survey year from 1985 through 2024 is processed once into a compact parquet file, hosted as a public GitHub release asset, and downloaded a single time into a local cache after verification against a published SHA-256 checksum. Queries run through DuckDB, so pulling a handful of variables from a 300-plus column file is fast and repeat analyses never re-transfer data. read_brfss() returns a tibble; brfss_design() returns a ready-made srvyr design object carrying the correct weight, strata, and primary sampling units for that survey era.

Design correctness is the default. brfss_design() selects _FINALWT before 2011 and _LLCPWT after, and refuses to pool years across the 2011 boundary unless you opt in explicitly. The codes CDC uses for "don't know" and "refused" arrive as NA, so proportions cover substantive answers. A variable crosswalk resolves CDC's renames across years, and the value-label codebook is bundled from 1998 onward, so question wording and factor levels are available without opening a PDF.

The hosted files are plain parquet at stable URLs, so the data are not locked inside R. Python, Julia, Stata, and DuckDB users can read the same files directly, and every year ships the design columns needed for weighted analysis elsewhere.
packages.use_cases:
- Pull respondent-level BRFSS records for one or many survey years without hand-downloading CDC ZIP archives
- Produce national or state-level prevalence estimates with correct weights, strata, and primary sampling units
- Track a health behavior or outcome across years, with the 2011 methodology break flagged rather than silently crossed
- Find which years carry a variable and what CDC renamed it to, via brfss_vars() and brfss_crosswalk()
- Look up value labels and question wording without opening a PDF codebook, via brfss_labels() and brfss_codebook()
- Restrict to specific states inside the query rather than after loading the full year
- Teach complex survey analysis on a real, large, public dataset that loads in seconds
- Read the same hosted parquet files from Python, Julia, Stata, or DuckDB with no R involved
packages.similar_packages:
nhanesA and nhanesdata do for NHANES what brfssdata does for BRFSS: bring a CDC survey's microdata into R. Different survey, different design, no overlap in coverage.

tidycensus and censusapi follow the same access pattern for Census and ACS data.

cdcfluview and epidatr surface CDC and Delphi surveillance data, but as aggregate indicators rather than respondent-level microdata.

survey and srvyr are the analysis layer brfssdata hands off to, not alternatives to it. brfssdata builds the design object; srvyr runs the estimate.

No other CRAN package provides BRFSS access. A name search across the full CRAN index returns brfssdata alone.
packages.unique_features:
It is the only CRAN package for BRFSS, and coverage is complete: all 40 published survey years, 1985 through 2024. CDC no longer serves the 1984 file, so the collection begins where the available data begin.

Three things separate it from a download-and-read script:

Survey-design correctness is built in. Weights, strata, and PSUs are applied automatically per survey era, the 2011 methodology break is a guard rather than a footnote, and CDC's missing-type codes become NA by default. Getting these wrong is the most common error in published BRFSS analyses, and here it takes deliberate effort to get wrong.

Transfers happen once. A year downloads a single time, is checksum-verified, and is cached under tools::R_user_dir(). DuckDB handles column selection and state filtering inside the query, so a two-variable extract from a 300-column survey does not move 300 columns. One cache directory can serve a whole lab or cluster, and the workflow runs fully offline after a prefetch.

The data stay open. Files are plain parquet at stable public URLs, readable from Python, Julia, Stata, or DuckDB without R. The conversion is faithful to CDC's source: no rows dropped, no columns dropped, no values recoded. The only changes are re-encoding legacy Windows-1252 text to UTF-8, storing blank SAS character fields as nulls, adding a year column, and giving the handful of variables CDC stored as numeric in some years and text in others one consistent storage type. The full processing pipeline is public in data-raw/, and every artifact is checksummed.
